paper.title: Damage-induced reactive oxygen species regulate vimentin and dynamic collagen-based projections to mediate wound repair
paper.abstract: Tissue injury leads to early wound-associated reactive oxygen species (ROS) production that mediate tissue regeneration. To identify mechanisms that function downstream of redox signals that modulate regeneration, a vimentin reporter of mesenchymal cells was generated by driving GFP from the vimentin promoter in zebrafish. Early redox signaling mediated vimentin reporter activity at the wound margin. Moreover, both ROS and vimentin were necessary for collagen production and reorganization into projections at the leading edge of the wound. Second harmonic generation time-lapse imaging revealed that the collagen projections were associated with dynamic epithelial extensions at the wound edge during wound repair. Perturbing collagen organization by burn wound disrupted epithelial projections and subsequent wound healing. Taken together our findings suggest that ROS and vimentin integrate early wound signals to orchestrate the formation of collagen-based projections that guide regenerative growth during efficient wound repair.

nodes.label: Vimentin functions downstream of wound-induced ROS/NFκB signaling to regulate co…
nodes.claim: Vimentin functions downstream of wound-induced ROS/NFκB signaling to regulate collagen expression and reorganization into projections that physically guide epithelial cell extensions, thereby promoting caudal fin regeneration in zebrafish larvae.
nodes.verbatim_quote: vimentin functions downstream of wound-induced redox signaling and regulates collagen expression and reorganization during wound repair...collagen projections at the wound edge guide epithelial growth during fin regeneration, a process dependent on vimentin.

strengths: The paper provides a multi-level analysis spanning ROS → NFκB → vimentin → collagen → epithelial projections → regeneration, with evidence at each step.
Multiple independent approaches (MO, CRISPR, pharmacological inhibition, burn model) converge on the same conclusion.
Live imaging of SHG fibers and epithelial cells provides compelling visual evidence of the collagen-epithelial projection association.
Consistent with Eckes et al. (2000) and Cheng et al. (2016) showing vimentin is required for wound healing in mice.
Consistent with Yoo et al. (2012) showing early ROS signaling is required for fin regeneration.
weaknesses: The 'pathway' is largely correlative — the paper does not establish direct mechanistic links between each step (e.g., no evidence that NFκB directly activates the vimentin promoter, no chromatin or binding studies).
The claim that collagen projections 'physically guide' epithelial extensions is based on correlative imaging rather than direct mechanical manipulation or force measurements.
WA is acknowledged to directly inhibit vimentin protein, confounding the NFκB → vimentin arm of the pathway.
DPI is a non-specific inhibitor that affects multiple flavoenzymes beyond NADPH oxidase, making ROS specificity questionable.
The CRISPR experiments use mosaic F0 mutants rather than stable knockouts, so the degree of vimentin loss is variable and not well quantified at the protein level.
No rescue of the collagen/projection phenotype specifically (only regenerate area rescue shown with vimentin RNA), limiting conclusions about the full pathway.
The word 'physically guide' implies a mechanical mechanism, but no biomechanical evidence (force measurements, adhesion studies) is provided.
alternative_interpretations: The collagen fibers and epithelial projections may both be downstream consequences of vimentin's role in mesenchymal cell function, rather than collagen physically guiding epithelial cells.

ROS may regulate multiple parallel pathways affecting regeneration (e.g., Wnt/FGF as shown by Love et al. (2013) in tadpoles), and the vimentin pathway may be one of several contributors rather than the primary mediator.
The projection phenotype could reflect general tissue health/growth rate differences rather than a specific guidance mechanism.
required_assumptions: That correlative imaging of SHG fibers and epithelial projections reflects a causal, physically guided mechanism.
That the pharmacological and MO/CRISPR tools are sufficiently specific to attribute effects to the named targets.
That the pathway is linear (ROS → NFκB → vimentin → collagen → projections → regeneration) rather than involving extensive cross-talk or parallel pathways.
That zebrafish larval fin regeneration mechanisms are generalizable.
evaluation.notes: This is a compelling correlative study with impressive live imaging, but the causal and mechanistic claims exceed what the evidence strictly demonstrates. The 'physical guidance' claim is the weakest link in the chain.

nodes.label: Wounding induces a population of vimentin-positive cells at the wound edge, and …
nodes.claim: Wounding induces a population of vimentin-positive cells at the wound edge, and this vimentin expression is regulated by early wound-induced ROS signaling through NFκB.
nodes.verbatim_quote: early redox signaling at the wound was required for vimentin expression at the wound margin

strengths: Both WMISH and the Tg(-2vim:egfp) reporter show wound-induced vimentin expression at the wound edge by 24 hpw, providing two independent lines of evidence.
Both pharmacological (DPI) and genetic (Duox1 MO) ROS inhibition reduce vimentin reporter activity, supporting ROS dependence.
The ROS → NFκB connection is supported by prior work from de Oliveira et al. (2014) showing wound-induced ROS regulates NFκB in zebrafish.
weaknesses: The NFκB arm relies entirely on Withaferin A, which the authors acknowledge also directly inhibits vimentin protein — this is a critical confound that undermines the NFκB specificity claim.
No NFκB-specific genetic tools (e.g., dominant negative NFκB, NFκB subunit morpholinos) were used to confirm the NFκB involvement.
DPI is non-specific (inhibits multiple flavoenzymes), so the 'ROS' attribution is not clean.
The quantification of vimentin reporter activity at the wound edge (Figure 2J) has relatively small sample sizes (n=12 total fins across three replicates) with modest effect sizes.
No direct evidence that NFκB binds or activates the vimentin promoter — the connection is entirely correlative via pharmacological inhibition.
alternative_interpretations: DPI may affect non-ROS pathways that regulate vimentin expression.
WA may reduce reporter activity by directly affecting vimentin protein stability/turnover rather than through NFκB-mediated transcriptional effects.
ROS may regulate vimentin through other redox-sensitive transcription factors beyond NFκB.
required_assumptions: That DPI specifically inhibits wound-induced ROS at the concentrations used.
That WA's effect on vimentin reporter activity is primarily through NFκB inhibition rather than direct vimentin protein effects.
That the Tg(-2vim:egfp) reporter faithfully reflects endogenous vimentin transcription dynamics.
evaluation.notes: The ROS → vimentin link is reasonably supported by multiple approaches, but the NFκB intermediate is weakly established due to the WA confound and lack of genetic NFκB manipulation.

nodes.label: Vimentin is required for proper wound healing and fin regeneration in zebrafish …
nodes.claim: Vimentin is required for proper wound healing and fin regeneration in zebrafish larvae.
nodes.verbatim_quote: vimentin-deficient larvae had impaired regenerate area and regenerate length at 3 dpw, indicating that vimentin is required for proper wound healing.

strengths: Multiple independent loss-of-function approaches converge: MO1, MO2, RNA rescue, and CRISPR F0 mosaic mutants all support the same conclusion.
Large sample sizes with strong statistical significance (p<0.0001 for both MO and CRISPR experiments).
Wound-specific defect confirmed — no developmental fin defect in unwounded vimentin-deficient larvae.
TUNEL staining rules out cell survival as the mechanism.
Consistent with Eckes et al. (2000) and Cheng et al. (2016) showing vimentin is required for wound healing in mice.
weaknesses: CRISPR F0 mosaic mutants have variable and unquantified levels of vimentin knockdown — protein-level validation is absent.
The MO rescue experiment is mentioned but detailed quantification is in supplementary figures; the rescue appears partial.
No stable vimentin knockout line was generated, which would provide definitive proof.
TUNEL was only assessed at 1 hpw, which is very early — later apoptosis effects cannot be ruled out.
The CRISPR mutants showed a slight increase in developmental fin area (Figure 3—figure supplement 3G), which is unexplained and potentially confounding.
alternative_interpretations: Morpholino off-target effects, while partially addressed by rescue and second MO, cannot be completely excluded.
The regeneration defect could reflect broader developmental/growth defects not captured by the fin measurements at 5 dpf.
required_assumptions: That morpholinos and CRISPR F0 mosaics provide sufficient knockdown of functional vimentin protein.
That the 5 dpf developmental assessment adequately captures any latent developmental defects.
evaluation.notes: This is one of the best-supported claims in the paper, with multiple complementary approaches and large sample sizes. The main limitation is the lack of stable mutant lines.

nodes.label: During wound repair, collagen fiber projections form at the wound edge and physi…
nodes.claim: During wound repair, collagen fiber projections form at the wound edge and physically guide epithelial cell extensions to promote forward progression of the wound plane.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Live imaging demonstrated that these collagen projections guide epithelial regrowth during regeneration of the fin.

strengths: Live imaging combining SHG and epithelial fluorescence reporters provides compelling visual evidence of close apposition between extending collagen fibers and epithelial projections.
The temporal correlation — fibers extending first, with epithelial cells following — is suggestive of a guidance role.
Multiple imaging modalities (bright field, SHG, LC-PolScope, phalloidin, Tg(krt4:egfp-caax)) provide convergent observations.
The observation that projections do not occur during normal development strengthens the wound-specific nature of this phenomenon.
weaknesses: The claim of 'physical guidance' is fundamentally correlative — no direct evidence demonstrates that collagen fibers mechanically direct epithelial cells (e.g., no laser ablation of individual fibers, no force measurements, no integrin blocking experiments).
The time resolution (~15 min intervals for SHG) may be insufficient to definitively establish the temporal ordering of fiber extension versus epithelial extension.
The words 'push' and 'guide' imply mechanical force but no biomechanical measurements are provided.
The observation that fibers 'appeared to push the epithelial cells outward' (Figure 4—video 3) is a subjective interpretation of dynamic imaging data.
No quantification of the spatial relationship between fibers and epithelial cells is provided (e.g., distance measurements, contact analysis).
alternative_interpretations: Epithelial cells may extend projections independently through their own actin-based motility, with collagen merely providing a passive substrate rather than active guidance.
Both collagen reorganization and epithelial extension may be driven by an underlying common signal (e.g., from mesenchymal cells) rather than collagen guiding epithelium.
The apparent 'pushing' may reflect co-extension of both structures driven by cellular growth/proliferation rather than mechanical guidance.
required_assumptions: That the temporal and spatial correlation between collagen fiber extension and epithelial projection formation reflects a causal, physically guided relationship.
That the imaging resolution is sufficient to distinguish active guidance from passive co-localization.
That 'projections' are mechanistically distinct from general tissue outgrowth.
evaluation.notes: This is perhaps the most novel and interesting claim in the paper, but it is also the one where the evidence most clearly falls short of the mechanistic language used. The live imaging is technically impressive but the interpretation as 'physical guidance' is not rigorously demonstrated.

nodes.label: Vimentin regulates both collagen expression and the dynamic reorganization of co…
nodes.claim: Vimentin regulates both collagen expression and the dynamic reorganization of collagen fibers into projections at the wound edge.
nodes.verbatim_quote: inhibition of ROS, NFκB or depletion of vimentin impaired both collagen expression at the wound and the dynamic reorganization of collagen into projections.

strengths: qRT-PCR demonstrates both wound-induced increases in col1a1 and col2a1b and their reduction upon vimentin depletion, with appropriate statistical support.
SHG imaging provides quantitative analysis of collagen fiber organization (contour length, fiber angle) showing clear defects in vimentin morphants.
The Larp6 knockdown experiment provides a plausible mechanistic link for col1a1 regulation, consistent with Challa and Stefanovic (2011).
Consistent with Cheng et al. (2016) showing vimentin regulates collagen accumulation in mouse wounds.
weaknesses: The qRT-PCR measures mRNA levels from a ~500 µm tissue region, not specifically from vim+ cells, so the cellular source of collagen expression changes is unknown.
No protein-level collagen quantification is provided (only mRNA and SHG signal).

SHG detects fibrillar collagen (primarily type I/III), and the relationship between mRNA expression and mature SHG-detectable fibers is indirect with substantial post-translational processing steps in between.
The Larp6 result is incomplete — it only partially explains the vimentin effect (col1a1 but not col2a1b), and the regeneration phenotype is also partial (area but not length).
Cannot distinguish between direct regulation of collagen expression by vimentin versus indirect effects through altered cellular composition or behavior at the wound.
alternative_interpretations: Vimentin depletion may reduce collagen expression indirectly by impairing the recruitment, survival, or differentiation of collagen-producing cells rather than through direct mRNA regulation.
The SHG fiber disorganization could reflect defective fiber assembly/cross-linking rather than reduced expression per se.
Reduced collagen expression could be a consequence of impaired regeneration rather than a cause.
required_assumptions: That mRNA expression levels are a reasonable proxy for functional collagen protein deposition.
That the vim+ cells are the relevant source of collagen regulation (or at least influence collagen-producing cells).
That SHG contour length and fiber angle accurately capture the biologically relevant features of collagen organization.
evaluation.notes: The combined mRNA and SHG data make a reasonable case for vimentin regulating collagen, but the indirect nature of the measurements and inability to separate cause from consequence weaken the claim.

nodes.label: Disruption of collagen organization, either by inhibiting cross-linking or by th…
nodes.claim: Disruption of collagen organization, either by inhibiting cross-linking or by thermal injury, impairs epithelial projection formation and subsequent wound healing.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Treatments that disrupt collagen organization, such as inhibition of cross-linking or destruction of collagen fibers by thermal injury, diminished the formation of epithelial projections and subsequent wound healing was impaired.

strengths: Two independent approaches (BAPN chemical inhibition and burn model) both disrupt collagen and impair projections/healing, providing convergent evidence.
The burn model is creative and provides a mechanically distinct way to disrupt collagen organization.
Strong statistical support for reduced projections and healing in the burn model (p=0.0116 and p<0.0001 respectively).
SHG imaging clearly demonstrates the absence of collagen fibers at the burn wound edge.
weaknesses: BAPN caused lethality at 4-5 dpf, preventing 3 dpw analysis and raising toxicity concerns — the authors acknowledge this but still draw conclusions from the regeneration data.
BAPN increased contour length rather than decreasing it, which the authors explain as a measurement artifact but does not align with the vimentin MO data.
The burn model causes massive tissue damage beyond collagen disruption (thermal damage to cells, proteins, etc.), making it impossible to attribute the healing defect specifically to collagen loss.
No attempt to rescue collagen in the burn model (e.g., exogenous collagen application) to test whether collagen restoration rescues healing.
The burn and amputation wounds are fundamentally different types of injury, making the comparison of healing outcomes difficult to interpret.
alternative_interpretations: The burn wound healing defect could be due to thermal damage to cells, growth factors, or other ECM components rather than specifically to collagen disruption.
BAPN may affect cross-linking of non-collagen substrates (e.g., elastin), contributing to the observed phenotype through non-collagen mechanisms.
The absence of epithelial projections after burn could reflect general tissue damage severity rather than a specific requirement for collagen guidance.
required_assumptions: That the BAPN effects are primarily due to collagen cross-linking inhibition at the doses used.
That the burn wound specifically disrupts collagen organization while preserving enough tissue viability for meaningful comparison with amputation.
That the toxicity of BAPN does not confound the regeneration assessment at 2 dpw.
evaluation.notes: Both approaches are creative but have significant confounds. The burn model is particularly problematic because it cannot separate collagen disruption from general tissue damage. The BAPN toxicity is concerning.

nodes.label: The Tg(-2vim:egfp) reporter line faithfully recapitulates vimentin expression an…
nodes.claim: The Tg(-2vim:egfp) reporter line faithfully recapitulates vimentin expression and serves as a tool to track vimentin-positive mesenchymal cells in vivo.
nodes.verbatim_quote: the Tg(−2vim:egfp) line recapitulated previously published in situ vimentin expression data and vimentin was expressed in cells undergoing EMT, thereby providing a powerful tool to report vimentin promoter activity in larval zebrafish.

strengths: Reporter expression pattern matches previously published in situ hybridization data from Cerdà et al. (1998).
Expression in expected cell types: cranial ganglion cells, spinal cord neurons, opercle, fin mesenchymal cells.
Functional validation through oncogenic HRasV12-induced EMT, showing appropriate upregulation of the reporter.
Developmental expression pattern (2-somite stage onward) is consistent with known vimentin expression dynamics.
The reporter uses a 2 kb upstream promoter fragment, which is a reasonable size for promoter reporters.
weaknesses: Only 2 kb of the promoter is used, which may miss regulatory elements further upstream, in introns, or in enhancers elsewhere.
EGFP protein has a long half-life and may not accurately reflect dynamic changes in vimentin transcription (reporter may persist longer than endogenous mRNA).
The HRasV12 EMT experiment was observed in only two replicates with no quantification provided.
No comparison of reporter activity to endogenous vimentin protein levels (no anti-vimentin antibody staining).
The 2 kb promoter may not include all regulatory elements responsive to wound signals, potentially affecting wound-edge expression fidelity.
alternative_interpretations: The reporter may underestimate or overestimate vimentin expression dynamics due to the incomplete promoter fragment and GFP protein stability.
required_assumptions: That the 2 kb promoter region captures the essential regulatory elements for vimentin expression in the contexts studied.
That EGFP expression dynamics reasonably approximate endogenous vimentin transcription dynamics.
evaluation.notes: The reporter validation is solid for spatial expression pattern but limited for dynamic fidelity. The EMT validation is underpowered.

nodes.label: These results provide a pathway linking early ROS signaling to the physical and …
nodes.claim: These results provide a pathway linking early ROS signaling to the physical and mechanical processes of healing and regrowth, which may inform therapeutic strategies including collagen scaffold-based approaches for wound repair.
nodes.verbatim_quote: These results provide a pathway linking early ROS signaling to the physical and mechanical processes of healing and regrowth.

strengths: The paper does identify correlations at each step of the proposed pathway (ROS → vimentin → collagen → projections → healing).
The authors appropriately acknowledge the caveat that it remains unclear how these observations translate to mammalian wound healing.
The reference to clinical collagen scaffold approaches (Kim et al., 2016; Tracy et al., 2016) provides relevant context.
weaknesses: This is a speculative discussion claim that extends well beyond the direct evidence in the paper.
No therapeutic experiments were performed — no collagen scaffolds were tested, no interventions to promote ROS were applied.
The pathway linking ROS to 'physical and mechanical processes' is correlative at every step, not mechanistically demonstrated.
The translational relevance to human wound healing is explicitly acknowledged as unclear.
No direct evidence connects the findings to any clinical application.
alternative_interpretations: The pathway may be specific to larval zebrafish fin regeneration and may not operate in non-regenerative organisms.
ROS in human wounds are generally associated with chronic wound pathology (Dhall et al., 2014), so the beneficial role suggested here may not translate.
required_assumptions: That the zebrafish larval fin regeneration pathway has translational relevance to human wound healing.
That ROS-mediated pathways would have similar beneficial effects in mammalian wound contexts.
evaluation.notes: This is primarily a speculative discussion claim. While the authors are appropriately cautious, the claim as stated overstates the therapeutic implications of the data.

nodes.label: Tail transection induces localized vimentin expression at the wound edge by 24 h…
nodes.claim: Tail transection induces localized vimentin expression at the wound edge by 24 hours post wound, as shown by both in situ hybridization and live reporter imaging.
nodes.verbatim_quote: tail transection induced localized vimentin expression at the wound edge by 24 hr post wound (hpw)

strengths: Two independent methods — WMISH and live confocal imaging of the Tg(-2vim:egfp) reporter — both show wound-induced vimentin expression at the wound edge by 24 hpw.
Sense probe control shows no signal, validating the WMISH specificity.
Time-lapse imaging provides dynamic temporal resolution showing no signal at 2 hpw, emerging signal at 20 hpw, and enhanced signal at 26 hpw.
Results are consistent across experiments (two replicates for WMISH noted).
weaknesses: WMISH was observed in only two experiments — the sample size for this observation is not specified.
The reporter may not perfectly recapitulate endogenous expression dynamics (EGFP stability issues).
No quantification of the WMISH signal is provided.
required_assumptions: That WMISH and the reporter provide complementary and accurate readouts of vimentin expression.
evaluation.notes: Well-supported by two independent approaches. The temporal dynamics from live imaging are a nice addition.

nodes.label: The wound-induced vimentin-positive cells do not migrate to the wound from surro…
nodes.claim: The wound-induced vimentin-positive cells do not migrate to the wound from surrounding tissue but rather arise as a non-motile population at the wound edge that activates vimentin expression in situ.
nodes.verbatim_quote: the vim+ cells did not migrate to the wound from surrounding fin tissue but rather expression developed in what appeared to be a non-motile population of cells at the wound edge

strengths: Long-duration time-lapse confocal microscopy using the zWEDGI platform (Huemer et al., 2017) provides an appropriate method for this observation.
The authors appropriately note caveats about time resolution and the possibility of progenitor cell migration followed by vimentin activation.
weaknesses: The conclusion that cells are 'non-motile' is limited by the temporal resolution of the imaging (~12 min intervals) — cells could migrate between frames.
The spatial resolution may be insufficient to distinguish slow migration from in situ activation.

The authors explicitly state 'these data do not preclude the possibility that the vim+ cells are the result of an EMT event beyond the time resolution of our studies,' which substantially weakens the claim.
No cell tracking analysis or quantification of cell displacement is provided.
Without lineage tracing, the origin of the vim+ cells remains unknown.
alternative_interpretations: The vim+ cells could be slow-migrating cells that arrive and then activate vimentin expression.
The cells could arise from a local EMT event not captured at the imaging time resolution.
Resident mesenchymal progenitors could upregulate vimentin expression without any migration being required.
required_assumptions: That the imaging frequency and duration are sufficient to detect any migration that would occur.
That the absence of observed migration equals absence of migration.
evaluation.notes: The authors are appropriately cautious but the claim as stated is stronger than the evidence warrants. The negative result (no migration observed) is limited by the methodology.

nodes.label: Pharmacological inhibition of ROS (DPI) for 1 hour before and after wounding is …
nodes.claim: Pharmacological inhibition of ROS (DPI) for 1 hour before and after wounding is sufficient to impair vimentin expression at the wound edge at 1 day post wound.
nodes.verbatim_quote: inhibition of ROS for 1 hr before and 1 hr after wounding was sufficient to impair the appearance of vim+ cells at the wound edge 1 dpw

strengths: Consistent with Yoo et al. (2012) who showed the same DPI treatment window impairs fin regeneration.
Quantification shows statistically significant reduction (p=0.0282) in reporter intensity at the wound edge.
Corroborated by Duox1 MO knockdown showing similar effects.
weaknesses: The sample size is modest (n=12 total fins over three replicates) with 2-6 fins per treatment per replicate, which is quite low per replicate.
DPI is a non-specific NADPH oxidase inhibitor; off-target effects on other flavoenzymes cannot be excluded.
The effect size is modest — the 95% CIs for DMSO (1.18-1.33) and DPI (1.07-1.21) show overlap at the boundary.
The Duox1 MO results are shown only qualitatively in supplementary figures without quantification.
alternative_interpretations: DPI may impair general cellular signaling or health in the wound region, indirectly reducing vimentin expression.
The modest effect size could reflect incomplete inhibition rather than partial involvement of ROS.
required_assumptions: That DPI specifically inhibits wound-induced ROS at the doses and timing used.
That the 1 hr pre/post treatment window is sufficient to capture the relevant ROS signaling.
evaluation.notes: The DPI result is supported by Duox1 MO data, strengthening the ROS attribution, but both lines of evidence have limitations. Sample sizes are low.

nodes.label: ROS regulates vimentin expression at least in part through NFκB activity, as pha…
nodes.claim: ROS regulates vimentin expression at least in part through NFκB activity, as pharmacological inhibition of NFκB blocks vimentin reporter expression at the wound.
nodes.verbatim_quote: early ROS signaling, likely at least in part through NFκB activity, regulates vimentin promoter activation at 1 dpw following caudal fin amputation.

strengths: WA treatment does reduce vimentin reporter expression at the wound, as shown in supplementary figures.
The ROS → NFκB connection is supported by de Oliveira et al. (2014).
weaknesses: The authors explicitly acknowledge that WA directly inhibits vimentin protein, making it impossible to distinguish NFκB-mediated transcriptional effects from direct vimentin protein effects.
No NFκB-specific genetic tools (dominant negative, subunit knockdown) were used to confirm the NFκB involvement.
Only one pharmacological inhibitor (WA) was used for NFκB, with known off-target effects on vimentin — this is a fundamental confound.
The WA result is shown only in supplementary figures without quantification.
The claim of 'at least in part through NFκB' is hedged but still overstates the evidence given the confound.
alternative_interpretations: WA may reduce reporter activity by destabilizing vimentin protein rather than through NFκB inhibition.
Other redox-sensitive transcription factors (AP-1, Nrf2, HIF) may mediate the ROS → vimentin connection.
WA may have additional anti-inflammatory effects that indirectly affect the wound microenvironment.
required_assumptions: That WA's primary mechanism of action at the doses used is NFκB inhibition rather than direct vimentin inhibition.
That the vimentin promoter reporter (EGFP) is unaffected by WA's direct vimentin protein effects.
evaluation.notes: This is one of the weakest claims in the paper. The confound between WA's effects on NFκB and vimentin protein is critical and not adequately addressed. The use of a reporter (EGFP driven by the vimentin promoter) partially mitigates the protein stability concern since EGFP protein should not be directly affected by WA, but transcriptional feedback from vimentin protein levels could still confound the result.

nodes.label: The vimentin-positive cells at the wound are not epithelial cells, not macrophag…
nodes.claim: The vimentin-positive cells at the wound are not epithelial cells, not macrophages, and their presence is not dependent on leukocytes.
nodes.verbatim_quote: these vim+ cells did not appear to arise from epithelial cells based on live imaging...the vim+ cells did not appear to colocalize with a macrophage marker...their presence was not influenced by the depletion of leukocytes

strengths: Multiple exclusion experiments: no co-localization with krt4 (epithelial), mpeg1:dendra2 (macrophage), and pu.1 MO (leukocyte depletion).
Uses appropriate transgenic lines for cell type identification.
3D reconstruction of time-lapse imaging provides spatial resolution for co-localization assessment.
weaknesses: The exclusions are based on specific markers rather than comprehensive cell typing — vim+ cells could be a different immune cell type not marked by mpeg1, or a different epithelial subtype not expressing krt4.
The positive identity of the vim+ cells is never established — only negative exclusions are provided.
The pu.1 MO experiment suggests leukocytes are not 'directly or indirectly' involved, but this is a very strong conclusion from a single MO experiment.
No single-cell transcriptomics or other comprehensive cell typing approaches were used.
The authors acknowledge the possibility that progenitor cells could be involved but cannot confirm or deny this.
alternative_interpretations: The vim+ cells could be tissue-resident fibroblasts, progenitor cells, or another mesenchymal cell type not tested.
Some immune cell types (e.g., neutrophils, dendritic cells) were not specifically excluded.
required_assumptions: That the markers used (krt4, mpeg1, pu.1) are comprehensive enough to exclude the relevant cell types.
That absence of co-localization reflects absence of cell type identity rather than marker expression variability.
evaluation.notes: The negative exclusions are informative but the positive identity of vim+ cells remains unknown, which is a significant gap for understanding the mechanism.

nodes.label: Vimentin-positive cells in the unwounded fin are tightly associated with SHG col…
nodes.claim: Vimentin-positive cells in the unwounded fin are tightly associated with SHG collagen fibers, and in wounded fins, rounded vim+ cells are observed in regions of collagen misalignment.
nodes.verbatim_quote: We observed a tight association between the vim+ cells and the SHG fibers...vim+ cells with a more rounded morphology in regions of the fin characterized by mis-aligned SHG collagen fibers

strengths: SHG imaging combined with fluorescence from Tg(-2vim:egfp) provides direct visualization of the spatial relationship.
3D surface rendering and videos clearly show vim+ cell alignment along SHG fibers in unwounded fins.
The morphological change of vim+ cells (elongated → rounded) in regions of collagen misalignment at the wound is an interesting and well-documented observation.
The observation is consistent with known interactions between mesenchymal cells (fibroblasts) and collagen fibers.
weaknesses: The association is purely descriptive — no functional experiments test whether the vim+ cell-collagen association is causal in either direction.
Assessed in only two replicates including 24 live larvae for wounded fins.
The resolution may be insufficient to determine whether vim+ cells are physically contacting collagen fibers or merely in proximity.
No quantification of the association (e.g., distance measurements, co-localization coefficients) is provided.
alternative_interpretations: The association may reflect shared spatial constraints (both cells and fibers are oriented by tissue architecture) rather than direct interaction.
The morphological change at the wound could reflect response to tissue damage/inflammation rather than specifically to collagen alignment.
required_assumptions: That SHG faithfully represents the collagen fibers that vim+ cells interact with.
That spatial association implies functional interaction.
evaluation.notes: Descriptively compelling but lacks functional validation of the association.

nodes.label: Morpholino depletion of vimentin impairs regenerate area and length at 3 days po…
nodes.claim: Morpholino depletion of vimentin impairs regenerate area and length at 3 days post wound.
nodes.verbatim_quote: vimentin-deficient larvae had impaired regenerate area and regenerate length at 3 dpw

strengths: Large sample size (n=85 per treatment over four replicates) with strong statistical significance (p<0.0001).
Both regenerate area and length are impaired, showing consistent defect.
95% confidence intervals do not overlap, indicating a robust effect.
weaknesses: Only morpholino knockdown — this single claim relies on MO1 alone, though other experiments in the paper use MO2 and CRISPR for additional support (see c1.2.2).
No protein-level validation of vimentin knockdown efficiency is shown (only RT-PCR in supplement).
required_assumptions: That the morpholino achieves sufficient and specific vimentin knockdown.
evaluation.notes: Well-powered experiment with clear results.

nodes.label: CRISPR-Cas9 mosaic F0 vimentin mutants also display reduced regenerate length an…
nodes.claim: CRISPR-Cas9 mosaic F0 vimentin mutants also display reduced regenerate length and area, confirming the morpholino result.
nodes.verbatim_quote: The mosaic F0 mutants also displayed reduced regenerate length and area at 3 dpw

strengths: Provides independent genetic confirmation of the MO result using CRISPR-Cas9.
Large sample sizes (ctrl n=130, Vim n=119) with strong statistical significance (p<0.0001).
Mutation validated by TOPO cloning and sequencing.
Germline sequencing from F0 adults provides additional validation.
weaknesses: F0 mosaic mutants have highly variable mutant allele frequencies — some cells will be wild-type, others heterozygous, others homozygous mutant.
No quantification of mutagenesis efficiency per larva (e.g., % mutant alleles) is provided.
No protein-level assessment of vimentin loss in the mosaics.
Only one CRISPR guide RNA was used — could have off-target effects.

The effect size in CRISPR mutants (ctrl CI: 110643-115689 vs Vim CI: 90275-95555) is smaller than in morphants (ctrl CI: 94604-101337 vs vim CI: 60551-67370), which may reflect mosaicism but also raises questions about specificity.
alternative_interpretations: The smaller effect size in CRISPR mosaics compared to MO could reflect either mosaicism or that the MO has off-target effects contributing to the phenotype.
required_assumptions: That the F0 mosaic approach provides sufficiently consistent vimentin disruption across larvae.
That one guide RNA is sufficient to avoid attributing CRISPR off-target effects.
evaluation.notes: Good confirmatory approach but the mosaic nature limits interpretive power. A stable knockout line would be much stronger.

nodes.label: The wound healing defect is wound-specific and not developmental, as vimentin-de…
nodes.claim: The wound healing defect is wound-specific and not developmental, as vimentin-deficient larvae show no defect in fin length or area during normal development.
nodes.verbatim_quote: This defect was wound-specific, as unwounded morphants did not display a defect in fin length or area compared to age matched controls during normal development

strengths: Direct comparison of unwounded vimentin-deficient and control larvae at 5 dpf shows no difference in fin length or area.
Demonstrated for both MO and CRISPR approaches (though CRISPR showed a slight increase in fin area, see Figure 3—figure supplement 3G).
weaknesses: The CRISPR F0 mosaics showed a slight increase in developmental fin area (Figure 3—figure supplement 3G), which is unexplained and somewhat contradicts the 'no developmental defect' claim.
Only fin length and area were assessed — other developmental parameters could be affected.
The developmental assessment at 5 dpf may be too early to detect latent defects.
alternative_interpretations: The slight increase in fin area in CRISPR mosaics could indicate that vimentin does have developmental roles that partially confound wound healing interpretation.
required_assumptions: That fin length and area at 5 dpf are sufficient indicators of normal development.
evaluation.notes: The slight developmental fin area increase in CRISPR mosaics should have been discussed more thoroughly.

nodes.label: The wound healing defect in vimentin-deficient larvae is not due to changes in c…
nodes.claim: The wound healing defect in vimentin-deficient larvae is not due to changes in cell survival, as no defect in apoptosis was detected at 1 hour post wound.
nodes.verbatim_quote: No defect was observed in the vimentin-deficient larvae at 1 hpw...providing evidence that the wound healing defect is likely not due to changes in cell survival.

strengths: TUNEL staining provides a standard method for assessing apoptosis.
The result at 1 hpw is informative for the immediate wound response.
weaknesses: TUNEL was assessed only at 1 hpw, which is very early — apoptosis differences could emerge later (e.g., 6, 12, 24 hpw).
No quantification of the TUNEL staining is provided — just qualitative 'no defect observed.'
Cell survival encompasses more than apoptosis (necrosis, ferroptosis, etc.) — TUNEL only assesses apoptosis.
The claim that 'the wound healing defect is likely not due to changes in cell survival' based on a single time point is an overinterpretation.
alternative_interpretations: Vimentin depletion could affect cell survival at later time points not assessed.
Non-apoptotic cell death mechanisms could contribute to the wound healing defect.
required_assumptions: That 1 hpw is the relevant time point for detecting survival differences.
That TUNEL is a comprehensive assay for cell survival.
evaluation.notes: A single time point TUNEL assay is insufficient to conclude that cell survival is unaffected. Multiple time points and quantification would be needed.

nodes.label: Epithelial cell projections form at the wound edge beginning around 18 hours pos…
nodes.claim: Epithelial cell projections form at the wound edge beginning around 18 hours post wound and become prominent by 24 hours post wound; these projections are not present during normal fin development.
nodes.verbatim_quote: The first visible projections after tail transection could be identified at 18 hpw and became prominent by 24 hpw...The formation of these epithelial extensions...was not present during normal development of the caudal fin

strengths: Time-lapse bright field microscopy (10 min intervals) provides direct visualization of projection formation dynamics.
Clear temporal characterization: first visible at 18 hpw, prominent by 24 hpw.
The distinction from normal development (smooth fin edge) is an important control observation.
weaknesses: The observation that projections are not present during normal development is from 'a single experiment' (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
No quantification of projection morphology (length, width, number) is provided beyond the binary presence/absence scoring.
required_assumptions: That bright field imaging provides sufficient resolution to identify projections accurately.
evaluation.notes: Well-documented observational finding with appropriate developmental control.

nodes.label: Fibrillar collagen structures protrude into the tips of the epithelial projectio…
nodes.claim: Fibrillar collagen structures protrude into the tips of the epithelial projections, and SHG fibers appear to push epithelial cells outward during extension of the wound edge.
nodes.verbatim_quote: the SHG fibers appeared to push the epithelial cells outward during extension of the wound edge

strengths: Multiple imaging modalities converge: bright field, LC-PolScope, SHG, phalloidin staining, and Tg(krt4:egfp-caax) all show consistent fiber-epithelial cell association.
The LC-PolScope observation of elongated, stretched cell membranes around fibers is suggestive of mechanical interaction.
Time-lapse SHG/fluorescence imaging provides dynamic evidence of co-extension.
weaknesses: The claim that fibers 'push' epithelial cells is interpretive — no force measurements are provided.
The temporal resolution (~15 min) may be insufficient to establish which structure extends first.
No perturbation experiments specifically test the pushing/guidance hypothesis (e.g., laser ablation of individual fibers to see if epithelial projections retract).
The stretched membrane appearance in LC-PolScope could reflect birefringence artifacts rather than mechanical stretching.
alternative_interpretations: Epithelial cells may actively migrate along collagen fibers through integrin-based adhesion rather than being passively 'pushed.'
Both structures may be driven outward by underlying tissue growth/cell division.
required_assumptions: That the spatial and temporal correlation between fiber extension and epithelial stretching reflects a mechanical interaction.
That stretched membranes in LC-PolScope images indicate mechanical force rather than imaging artifacts.
evaluation.notes: The imaging evidence is compelling but the mechanistic interpretation of 'pushing' exceeds what the data directly demonstrate.

nodes.label: The fibers in the projections are organized collagen structures, as confirmed by…
nodes.claim: The fibers in the projections are organized collagen structures, as confirmed by polarization microscopy (LC-PolScope), SHG imaging, and collagen type II immunolabeling.
nodes.verbatim_quote: This observation of fibrillar structures was supported by LC-PolScope microscopy suggesting that the fibrillar protein was a collagen structure.

strengths: SHG detects fibrillar collagen (primarily type I/III), providing direct molecular identification (Campagnola et al., 2002).
Col II immunofluorescence co-localizes with SHG fibers in both unwounded and wounded fins.
LC-PolScope detection of birefringent fibers is consistent with organized collagen.
The observation of Col II caps at broken SHG fiber tips is an interesting structural finding.
weaknesses: SHG is not exclusively specific to collagen — other organized structures could contribute to signal.
No direct biochemical analysis (mass spectrometry, Western blot of purified fibers) confirms collagen composition.
The Col II immunofluorescence specificity in zebrafish larvae was not validated with controls (knockout, blocking peptide).
alternative_interpretations: Some SHG signal could come from non-collagen organized structures (e.g., organized actin or other fibrillar proteins).
required_assumptions: That SHG signal in the zebrafish fin is primarily from collagen.
That the Col II antibody is specific in zebrafish larvae.
evaluation.notes: Multiple converging methods strongly support the collagen identification.

literature_citations.title: SHG imaging of collagen
literature_citations.relevance: Established SHG as a method for detecting fibrillar collagen (type I/III).

nodes.label: Vimentin depletion impairs the formation of epithelial projections: vimentin-def…
nodes.claim: Vimentin depletion impairs the formation of epithelial projections: vimentin-deficient larvae display a smooth wound edge and fewer projections at 24 hours post wound.
nodes.verbatim_quote: vimentin-deficient larvae possessed a smooth wound edge and relative absence of the epithelial projections for more than 24 hpw

strengths: Quantification shows clear difference: >75% of controls vs ~40% of vimentin morphants display projections at 24 hpw.
Statistical significance achieved (p=0.0348).
Time-lapse videos (Figure 4—videos 1 and 2) provide dynamic visual evidence of the smooth wound edge in morphants.
weaknesses: The confidence intervals for vimentin MO projections (7.56-65.78%) are very wide, indicating high variability across replicates.
Only n=3 replicate percentages were compared — the statistical test compares three proportions per group, not individual larvae.
The p-value (0.0348) is near the significance threshold.
Projection assessment appears to be binary (present/absent) and subjective — no blinding is mentioned for scoring.
The ~40% of vim morphants that DO form projections is not discussed — this suggests the effect is incomplete.
alternative_interpretations: The partial effect (40% still forming projections) could indicate that vimentin is not the sole regulator or that MO knockdown is incomplete.
Delayed rather than absent projection formation could explain the result.
required_assumptions: That binary scoring of projection presence is objective and reliable.
That the timing window assessed (24 hpw) is the most informative.
evaluation.notes: The wide CI for vimentin MO and the near-threshold p-value are concerning. The incomplete penetrance should have been discussed.

nodes.label: Early pharmacological inhibition of ROS also impairs epithelial projection forma…
nodes.claim: Early pharmacological inhibition of ROS also impairs epithelial projection formation at 24 hours post wound.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Early pharmacological inhibition of ROS resulted in a smooth wound edge and impaired the formation of projections at 24 hpw

strengths: DPI treatment significantly reduces projection formation (p=0.0129).
Consistent with the ROS → vimentin → projection pathway proposed.
WA treatment shows similar results, providing additional pharmacological support.
weaknesses: The DMSO control CI (31.76-99.58%) is extremely wide, indicating enormous variability in the control group across replicates.
With such wide CIs and only n=3 replicate percentages, the statistical power is questionable.
Both DPI and WA are non-specific inhibitors with multiple targets.
The wide variability in controls suggests the assay itself may not be robust.
alternative_interpretations: DPI may affect epithelial cell motility or other processes independent of the vimentin pathway.
The high variability in controls may reflect uncontrolled experimental variables.
required_assumptions: That DPI's effects are primarily through ROS inhibition.
That the binary scoring method is sufficiently reproducible.
evaluation.notes: The extremely wide CI for the DMSO control (31.76-99.58%) is a red flag for assay reproducibility.

nodes.label: Vimentin depletion reduces collagen fiber projections at the wound edge, as meas…
nodes.claim: Vimentin depletion reduces collagen fiber projections at the wound edge, as measured by reduced wound edge contour length in SHG imaging.
nodes.verbatim_quote: The vimentin-deficient larvae had a reduced contour length at the wound edges as compared to control larvae

strengths: Good sample sizes (ctrl n=33, vim n=32 over 4 replicates) with strong statistical significance (p=0.0009).
Non-overlapping 95% CIs support a clear reduction.
Quantitative SHG analysis provides objective measurement.
3D rotating videos supplement the quantitative analysis.
weaknesses: Contour length is a relatively crude measure — it could be affected by wound shape differences unrelated to fiber projections.
The measurement was taken from Z-projections of a specific region, which may not capture the full 3D structure.
alternative_interpretations: Reduced contour length could reflect generally delayed healing rather than a specific effect on fiber projections.
required_assumptions: That wound contour length in SHG images is a valid proxy for fiber projection formation.
evaluation.notes: Well-quantified and adequately powered.

nodes.label: Vimentin depletion causes collagen fibers to orient more parallel rather than pe…
nodes.claim: Vimentin depletion causes collagen fibers to orient more parallel rather than perpendicular to the wound edge, as quantified by CurveAlign analysis.
nodes.verbatim_quote: the population of fibers with vimentin depletion tended to be less perpendicular overall than their control counterparts

strengths: CurveAlign analysis provides an objective, automated quantification method (Bredfeldt et al., 2014).
Good sample sizes (ctrl n=30, vim n=32 over 4 replicates) with strong significance (p=0.0003).
The method quantifies fiber angle relative to the wound edge, which is the relevant geometric parameter.
Non-overlapping CIs support a clear effect.
weaknesses: The mean angle difference is modest (ctl: ~68.7° vs vim: ~61.8°) — the biological significance of a ~7° shift is unclear.
CurveAlign was developed for mammographic collagen analysis and its validation in zebrafish SHG images is not discussed.
The analysis was restricted to fibers within 60 µm of the wound edge — different distance thresholds could yield different results.
alternative_interpretations: The angle change could reflect wound geometry differences rather than specific fiber reorganization defects.
The modest shift may not be functionally meaningful for guiding epithelial projections.
required_assumptions: That CurveAlign analysis is appropriate for zebrafish SHG images.
That the 60 µm threshold captures the relevant region.
That mean fiber angle is a meaningful metric for guidance capability.
evaluation.notes: Technically rigorous quantification, though the biological significance of the angle difference warrants discussion.

literature_citations.title: CurveAlign software for fiber analysis
literature_citations.relevance: Provided the analytical tool used for fiber angle quantification.

nodes.label: Vimentin depletion reduces wound-induced expression of both col1a1 and col2a1b a…
nodes.claim: Vimentin depletion reduces wound-induced expression of both col1a1 and col2a1b at 24 hours post wound.
nodes.verbatim_quote: vimentin-deficient larvae displayed a reduction in col1a1 and col2a1b expression at 24 hpw compared to controls

strengths: qRT-PCR with appropriate wound-specific tissue sampling (500 µm from wound) shows clear reductions in both col1a1 (p=0.004) and col2a1b (p=0.0404).
Multiple biological replicates (n=5-6 per condition).
Consistent with Cheng et al. (2016) showing vimentin regulates collagen accumulation.
Both collagen types affected, suggesting a broad regulatory role.
weaknesses: mRNA levels may not reflect protein levels or mature collagen fiber deposition.
The tissue sample includes many cell types — cannot attribute expression changes to vim+ cells specifically.
col2a1b p=0.0404, which is near the significance threshold.
Cannot distinguish reduced expression from reduced numbers of collagen-producing cells.
alternative_interpretations: Reduced collagen mRNA could reflect fewer fibroblasts/osteoblasts at the wound rather than reduced per-cell expression.
Reduced collagen expression could be a consequence of impaired healing rather than a cause.
required_assumptions: That mRNA levels meaningfully predict collagen protein production.
That the tissue sampling strategy captures the relevant wound region consistently.
evaluation.notes: Solid qRT-PCR data but cannot establish cellular specificity or causality.

literature_citations.title: Vimentin regulates wound healing via TGFβ-Slug signaling
literature_citations.relevance: Prior evidence that vimentin regulates collagen accumulation at wounds.

nodes.label: Vimentin may regulate col1a1 expression through Larp6, as Larp6-deficient larvae…
nodes.claim: Vimentin may regulate col1a1 expression through Larp6, as Larp6-deficient larvae show reduced col1a1 expression and impaired regenerate area.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Larp6-deficient larvae have reduced col1a1 expression but no defect in col2a1b expression...Larp6-deficient larvae displayed a significant defect in regenerate area

strengths: Larp6 MO selectively reduces col1a1 but not col2a1b, exactly as predicted by Challa and Stefanovic (2011) in vitro data.
This selective effect provides evidence for a specific vimentin-Larp6-col1a1 axis operating in vivo.
Larp6 deficiency causes a regeneration defect (area), supporting functional relevance.
weaknesses: The Larp6 result only explains the col1a1 arm — the col2a1b regulation by vimentin remains unexplained.
Larp6 deficiency shows area but not length defect, which is a partial phenocopy suggesting additional mechanisms.
Larp6 regeneration data represents 'a single experiment performed in triplicate' — limited replication.
No rescue experiment for Larp6 MO.
The claim is hedged ('may regulate') appropriately given the indirect evidence.
alternative_interpretations: Vimentin may regulate col1a1 through mechanisms other than or in addition to Larp6.
The partial regeneration phenotype suggests Larp6 is not the sole downstream effector of vimentin.
required_assumptions: That the Larp6 MO achieves specific and sufficient knockdown.
That the in vitro vimentin-Larp6 interaction (Challa and Stefanovic, 2011) operates similarly in vivo in zebrafish.
evaluation.notes: Interesting mechanistic probe but limited by single experiment replication and partial phenotype.

literature_citations.title: Vimentin regulates collagen I mRNA through Larp6
literature_citations.relevance: Provided the mechanistic prediction that Larp6 mediates vimentin's effect on col1a1, which was validated in vivo here.

nodes.label: Early ROS inhibition also reduces collagen expression (col1a1 and col2a1b) and S…
nodes.claim: Early ROS inhibition also reduces collagen expression (col1a1 and col2a1b) and SHG fiber contour length at 24 hours post wound.
nodes.verbatim_quote: pharmacological inhibition of early ROS signaling was sufficient to cause a significant reduction in the rise of collagen expression following amputation at 24 hpw

strengths: DPI reduces both col1a1 (p=0.0464) and col2a1b (p=0.0126) expression at 24 hpw.
SHG contour length reduction is consistent with reduced collagen organization.
WA shows similar results, providing pharmacological convergence.
Links early ROS signaling to collagen expression at the wound.
weaknesses: DPI p-values are near significance threshold (especially col1a1 at p=0.0464).
DPI non-specificity means effects may not be solely ROS-mediated.
Only n=4 replicates for qRT-PCR.
Cannot distinguish whether reduced collagen expression is a direct downstream effect of ROS inhibition or secondary to impaired healing.
alternative_interpretations: DPI may reduce collagen expression by generally impairing wound healing processes, with collagen reduction being a downstream consequence rather than a specific ROS-mediated effect.
WA's effects may be through direct vimentin inhibition rather than NFκB.
required_assumptions: That the brief DPI treatment window specifically affects ROS signaling.
That collagen expression changes at 24 hpw are causally linked to early ROS signaling rather than reflecting general healing impairment.
evaluation.notes: Consistent with the overall narrative but borderline p-values and specificity concerns limit strength.

nodes.label: Inhibition of collagen cross-linking with BAPN impairs fin regeneration and disr…
nodes.claim: Inhibition of collagen cross-linking with BAPN impairs fin regeneration and disrupts fiber organization at the wound edge.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Constant inhibition of lysyl oxidase throughout the wound healing process caused a significant reduction in regeneration of the larval fin at 2 dpw

strengths: BAPN treatment reduced both regenerate area and length at 2 dpw, providing functional evidence.
SHG fiber angle analysis shows disorganization consistent with vimentin morphant phenotype.
Lysyl oxidase is a well-established target for collagen cross-linking inhibition.
weaknesses: BAPN caused lethality at 4-5 dpf, preventing longer-term assessment and raising toxicity concerns.
The authors acknowledge the effects could partly be due to toxicity.
BAPN paradoxically increased contour length, which the authors attribute to measurement artifact from V-shaped fins — this is not convincing without further validation.
Data from a 'single experiment performed in triplicate' limits replication confidence.
BAPN inhibits lysyl oxidase, which cross-links elastin in addition to collagen — effects may not be collagen-specific.
No dose-response experiments to establish a therapeutic window.
alternative_interpretations: BAPN effects on regeneration could be due to general toxicity rather than specific collagen cross-linking inhibition.
The V-shaped fins could reflect mechanical/structural defects beyond collagen cross-linking.
Elastin cross-linking inhibition could contribute to the phenotype.
required_assumptions: That BAPN at the used concentration primarily affects collagen cross-linking without significant toxicity at 2 dpw.
That the contour length increase is indeed a measurement artifact.
evaluation.notes: The toxicity issue significantly limits the interpretive power of this experiment. The paradoxical contour length increase further complicates interpretation.

nodes.label: Burn wounds destroy SHG fiber integrity near the wound edge, dramatically impair…
nodes.claim: Burn wounds destroy SHG fiber integrity near the wound edge, dramatically impair epithelial projection formation, and significantly reduce wound healing compared to tail transection.
nodes.verbatim_quote: burn wounds resulting in a loss of SHG fiber integrity led to a significant reduction in the percentage of larvae displaying epithelial projections at 24 hpb...the burn wound had significant defects in healing as compared to tail transection

strengths: SHG imaging clearly demonstrates absence of collagen fibers near the burn wound edge.
Strong statistical significance for both reduced projections (p=0.0116) and reduced healing area (p<0.0001).
The burn model provides a mechanically distinct approach to disrupting collagen, complementing genetic/pharmacological approaches.
Comparison with tail transection in the same experimental setup provides a strong internal control.
weaknesses: Burn wounds cause extensive tissue damage beyond collagen disruption — thermal damage to cells, proteins, lipids, etc. — making it impossible to attribute effects specifically to collagen loss.
The amputation and burn models are fundamentally different injury types with different amounts of tissue damage, making direct comparison problematic.
No attempt to rescue the burn wound phenotype by providing exogenous collagen or other interventions.
The healing area comparison (24-48 hpb vs hpw) uses different initial wound sizes and geometries.
Only two experiments were performed for several burn wound observations.
alternative_interpretations: The healing defect after burn could be due to thermal damage to cells and growth factors rather than collagen loss.
The absence of projections could reflect general cellular damage in the wound margin rather than specific collagen guidance loss.
Burn wounds may trigger different inflammatory responses that impede healing independently of collagen.
required_assumptions: That the primary relevant difference between burn and amputation wounds is collagen fiber integrity.
That the comparison between these fundamentally different wound types is valid.
evaluation.notes: Creative approach but severely limited by the inability to separate collagen disruption from general tissue damage. This is a significant confound that the authors do not adequately address.

nodes.label: Vimentin-positive cells appear at the burn wound edge but with different morphol…
nodes.claim: Vimentin-positive cells appear at the burn wound edge but with different morphology compared to tail transection, suggesting the wound microenvironment influences vim+ cell behavior.
nodes.verbatim_quote: vim+ cells also appeared at the wound edge in the burn wound, although the morphology of the cells were different compared to tail transection

strengths: The observation that vim+ cells appear at burn wounds demonstrates that vimentin activation is a general wound response.
The morphological difference between burn and amputation vim+ cells is an interesting observation.
weaknesses: Observed in only two experiments with no quantification.
No analysis of what causes the morphological difference.
The claim about 'wound microenvironment influencing vim+ cell behavior' is speculative based on a qualitative observation.
No functional consequences of the different morphology are established.
alternative_interpretations: The morphological difference could reflect different cell types being activated in burn vs amputation wounds.
Heat damage could directly alter cell morphology independent of the wound microenvironment.
required_assumptions: That the same vim+ cell population is being observed in both wound types.
That the morphological difference reflects the wound microenvironment rather than direct thermal damage.
evaluation.notes: Interesting but preliminary observation that warrants further investigation.

nodes.label: The reporter recapitulates known vimentin expression in cranial ganglion cells, …
nodes.claim: The reporter recapitulates known vimentin expression in cranial ganglion cells, spinal cord neurons, opercle, and fin mesenchymal cells.
nodes.verbatim_quote: This expression pattern is consistent with the vimentin expression pattern previously shown by in situ hybridization

strengths: Expression matches published in situ data from Cerdà et al. (1998) in multiple cell types: cranial ganglion cells, spinal cord neurons, opercle.
Expression detected from the two-somite stage, consistent with known early vimentin expression.
Additional expression in fin mesenchymal cells at 3 dpf provides a novel but anatomically consistent observation.
weaknesses: Only qualitative comparison with published in situ data — no quantitative co-localization or systematic comparison.
Some expression domains may be absent due to the 2 kb promoter limitation.
required_assumptions: That the published in situ data from Cerdà et al. (1998) is accurate and comprehensive.
evaluation.notes: Solid validation against published data.

literature_citations.title: Vimentin in situ expression in zebrafish
literature_citations.relevance: The reference standard against which the reporter expression was validated.

nodes.label: Oncogenic HRasV12, but not wild-type HRasG12, induces vimentin promoter activity…
nodes.claim: Oncogenic HRasV12, but not wild-type HRasG12, induces vimentin promoter activity in the reporter line, confirming it reports EMT-associated vimentin expression.
nodes.verbatim_quote: Overexpression of oncogenic HRasV12, but not wild type HRasG12, induced vimentin promoter activity and expression of EGFP that co-localized in the same cells expressing HRasV12.

strengths: HRasV12 but not HRasG12 induces reporter activity, providing specificity for oncogenic (EMT-inducing) signaling.
Co-localization of EGFP and RFP-tagged HRasV12 in the same cells strengthens the result.
Consistent with known vimentin upregulation during EMT (Franke et al., 1982; Vuoriluoto et al., 2011).
weaknesses: Observed in only two replicates with no quantification.
Mosaic expression means only some cells are affected — no population-level analysis.
No negative control for spontaneous EGFP expression in uninjected larvae shown in this specific experiment.
The EMT induction by HRasV12 is well established (Freisinger and Huttenlocher, 2014) but the quantitative relationship between EMT and vimentin reporter activity is not characterized.
alternative_interpretations: HRasV12 may directly activate the vimentin promoter through Ras-responsive elements rather than through a full EMT program.
required_assumptions: That HRasV12 expression induces genuine EMT in this mosaic system.
That two replicates are sufficient for this validation.
evaluation.notes: Underpowered but the qualitative result is convincing given the clear specificity between G12 and V12.

literature_citations.title: HRasV12 induces EMT in zebrafish
literature_citations.relevance: Established the oncogenic Ras EMT model used for reporter validation.

nodes.label: ROS stimulates vimentin expression through NFκB, which is a known redox-sensitiv…
nodes.claim: ROS stimulates vimentin expression through NFκB, which is a known redox-sensitive transcription factor activated by wound-induced DUOX1/hydrogen peroxide.
nodes.verbatim_quote: We propose that ROS stimulates vimentin expression in a population of cells at the wound through its effects on NFκB activity. NFκB is known to be a redox sensitive transcription factor

strengths: The ROS → NFκB connection is supported by published work from de Oliveira et al. (2014) in the same zebrafish model.
NFκB is well-established as a redox-sensitive transcription factor (Nakajima and Kitamura, 2013).
DUOX1/H2O2-mediated NFκB activation in zebrafish larvae has been demonstrated.
weaknesses: This is a discussion claim that synthesizes published work with the current findings — the direct ROS → NFκB → vimentin pathway is not established in this paper.
The NFκB → vimentin link relies on WA, which has the confound of directly inhibiting vimentin protein.
No direct evidence (ChIP, promoter analysis) shows NFκB binds or activates the vimentin promoter.
The claim of a linear ROS → NFκB → vimentin pathway may oversimplify a complex signaling network.
alternative_interpretations: ROS may activate vimentin through multiple parallel transcription factors, with NFκB being only one contributor.
NFκB may regulate vimentin indirectly through other transcriptional targets that then influence vimentin expression.
required_assumptions: That NFκB is the primary (or at least a significant) mediator between ROS and vimentin expression.
That the WA-based evidence for NFκB involvement is valid despite the confound.
evaluation.notes: A reasonable synthesis claim but the direct mechanistic evidence is weaker than the discussion implies.

literature_citations.title: NFκB activation in zebrafish larvae following wounding
literature_citations.relevance: Demonstrated wound-induced DUOX1/H2O2 activates NFκB in zebrafish larvae.

literature_citations.title: NFκB as redox-sensitive transcription factor
literature_citations.relevance: Established NFκB as a redox-sensitive transcription factor, supporting the proposed pathway.

nodes.label: These findings suggest that redox signaling may have beneficial effects on the E…
nodes.claim: These findings suggest that redox signaling may have beneficial effects on the ECM in the wound microenvironment, which may be relevant to human wound healing beyond just detrimental effects.
nodes.verbatim_quote: It is interesting to speculate that this may also be the case in humans, rather than just having the detrimental effects suggested by some clinical studies

strengths: The authors appropriately use hedging language ('it is interesting to speculate').
The zebrafish data do show beneficial effects of ROS on wound ECM in a regenerative context.
weaknesses: This is pure speculation with no human data or cross-species validation.
The paper's own findings are in a larval zebrafish, an organism with fundamentally different wound healing capacity than humans.
Clinical literature on ROS and wound healing presents a complex picture that cannot be addressed by zebrafish data alone.
No experiments test whether ROS-mediated collagen effects are conserved beyond zebrafish.
alternative_interpretations: ROS in human wounds may have context-dependent effects (beneficial in acute wounds, detrimental in chronic wounds) that cannot be predicted from zebrafish data.
The regenerative capacity of zebrafish may enable beneficial ROS effects that would be pathological in non-regenerative species.
required_assumptions: That zebrafish regenerative mechanisms are conserved and relevant in human wound healing.
That ROS signaling has similar downstream effects on ECM in humans and zebrafish.
evaluation.notes: Purely speculative claim. Appropriately hedged but without evidentiary support in the paper.

nodes.label: It remains unclear how these observations in zebrafish larvae translate to mamma…
nodes.claim: It remains unclear how these observations in zebrafish larvae translate to mammalian wound healing.
nodes.verbatim_quote: a caveat is that it remains unclear how these observations translate to mammalian wound healing.

strengths: The authors appropriately acknowledge this limitation.
This is a factual statement about the state of knowledge, not a claim requiring evidence.

nodes.label: Whole mount in situ hybridization showed vimentin RNA expression at the wound ed…
nodes.claim: Whole mount in situ hybridization showed vimentin RNA expression at the wound edge at 24 hpw but not in unwounded fins; sense probe showed no signal.
nodes.verbatim_quote: we performed whole mount in situ hybridization (WMISH) to probe vimentin expression in unwounded and wounded larvae and found that tail transection induced localized vimentin expression at the wound edge by 24 hr post wound

strengths: WMISH with antisense probe shows wound-specific vimentin expression at 24 hpw.
Sense probe control shows no signal, confirming probe specificity.
Comparison between wounded and unwounded larvae is clear.
weaknesses: Only two experiments performed.
No quantification of WMISH signal.
WMISH images are in supplementary figures — the main figure description is brief.
required_assumptions: That WMISH probe specificity is adequate.
evaluation.notes: Standard technique, appropriately controlled.

nodes.label: Live confocal imaging of the Tg(-2vim:egfp) reporter showed no EGFP signal at th…
nodes.claim: Live confocal imaging of the Tg(-2vim:egfp) reporter showed no EGFP signal at the wound at 2 hpw, detectable signal by 20 hpw, and enhanced expression at 26 hpw.
nodes.verbatim_quote: no clear signal was detected along the wound edge at 2 hpw...vim+ cells were detected by 20 hpw at the wound edge and showed enhanced expression at 26 hpw

strengths: Live imaging provides temporal dynamics not possible with fixed tissue approaches.
Clear progression from no signal (2 hpw) to detectable (20 hpw) to enhanced (26 hpw).
